```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(patchwork)
library(palmerpenguins)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 18))
options(knitr.table.format = "html")
options(digits = 3)
set.seed(4)
# Palette: viridis for the primary scale, magma for the second one.
v_dark <- "#440154"; v_blue <- "#31688e"; v_teal <- "#21918c"; v_green <- "#5ec962"
m_pink <- "#b73779"; m_purple <- "#8c2981"; m_orange <- "#fc8961"
# A two-parameter quadratic valley, curvature 1 along beta_1 and 10 along beta_2,
# for the step-size pictures. Gradient descent on it is the exact recurrence
# beta_{t+1} = (1 - gamma a) beta_t in each coordinate.
fq <- function(b1, b2) 0.5 * (b1^2 + 10 * b2^2)
gd_path <- function(start, gamma, steps, a = c(1, 10)) {
  b <- start
  out <- matrix(NA, steps + 1, 2); out[1, ] <- b
  for (t in 1:steps) { b <- b - gamma * a * b; out[t + 1, ] <- b }
  tibble(step = 0:steps, b1 = out[, 1], b2 = out[, 2])
}
contour_grid <- expand_grid(b1 = seq(-4.5, 4.5, length.out = 121),
                            b2 = seq(-2.2, 2.2, length.out = 121)) |>
  mutate(f = fq(b1, b2))
contour_plot <- function(path, title = NULL) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_contour(data = contour_grid, aes(b1, b2, z = f),
                 breaks = c(0.25, 1, 2.5, 5, 10, 20), colour = "grey70") +
    geom_path(data = path, aes(b1, b2), colour = v_blue, linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_point(data = path, aes(b1, b2), colour = v_blue, size = 1.8) +
    geom_point(data = path[1, ], aes(b1, b2), colour = m_orange, size = 3) +
    coord_equal(xlim = c(-4.5, 4.5), ylim = c(-2.2, 2.2)) +
    labs(x = expression(beta[1]), y = expression(beta[2]), title = title) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16))
}
```

## Fitting logistic regression

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide with the recall box. Fisher: the method and the word, 1912 to 1922. The log changes nothing about where the maximum is. Least squares is the Gaussian log-likelihood, so lm is glm with family gaussian.
:::

::: {.recall}
**Maximum likelihood** (Fisher, 1912--1922): choose the parameter that makes the observed data most probable. We maximize the **log**-likelihood because a product of $n$ small numbers underflows and a sum differentiates term by term; log is increasing, so the maximizer is the same. **Least squares is a log-likelihood**: for $y_i \sim N(\mathbf x_i^\top\beta, \sigma^2)$ it is $-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i (y_i - \mathbf x_i^\top\beta)^2 + \text{const}$. In `glm`, `family` names the distribution whose likelihood is maximized: `gaussian` is `lm`, `binomial` is logistic regression.
:::

How do we estimate $\beta$? **Maximum likelihood**:

$$
\text{maximize } L(\beta ; \mathbf y | \mathbf X) = \prod_{i=1}^n L(\beta ; y_i | \mathbf x_i)
$$
(assuming the data is i.i.d.)

Next slide: a bit of mathematics

## MLE

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide. Each row is a Bernoulli; log turns the product into a sum.
:::

$$
L(\beta ; \mathbf y | \mathbf x) = \prod_{i=1}^n \left( \frac{1}{1+e^{-x_i \beta}} \right)^{y_i} \left(1- \frac{1}{1+e^{-x_i \beta}} \right)^{1-y_i}
$$

. . .

$$
\ell(\beta ; \mathbf y | \mathbf x) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ y_i \log \left( \frac{1}{1+e^{-x_i \beta}} \right) + (1-y_i) \log \left(1- \frac{1}{1+e^{- x_i \beta}} \right) \right]
$$

## MLE: the derivative

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide, continued. The last line is the one to remember: x times residual.
:::

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta} \ell(\beta ; \mathbf y | \mathbf x) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ y_i  \left( \frac{x_i e^{-x_i \beta}}{1+e^{-x_i \beta}} \right) + (1-y_i) \left(\frac{-x_i}{1+e^{- x_i \beta}} \right) \right]
$$

$$= \sum_{i=1}^n x_i \left[ y_i - \left(\frac{1}{1+e^{- x_i \beta}} \right) \right] = \color{#b73779}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i [y_i - \hat p_i(\beta)]}$$

Set this equal to 0 and solve for $\beta$. How: the rest of today

## The score equations, read as orthogonality

::: {.notes}
Derived, not proved: the derivative is on the previous slide, this slide reads it as a vector equation. Same shape as week 2.
:::

::: {.retrieval}
Week 2, least squares: $\mathbf X^\top(\mathbf y - \mathbf X\hat\beta) = \mathbf 0$. The residual is orthogonal to every column of $\mathbf X$.
:::

**Logistic score equations.** Stack the last slide's rows: writing $\mathbf p(\beta) = (\hat p_1(\beta), \ldots, \hat p_n(\beta))^\top$, the MLE $\hat\beta$ solves
$$
\mathbf X^\top\big(\mathbf y - \mathbf p(\hat\beta)\big) = \mathbf 0
$$

Same shape as least squares, with $\mathbf X\hat\beta$ replaced by the fitted probabilities: the residual $\mathbf y - \hat{\mathbf p}$ is orthogonal to every column of $\mathbf X$

No closed form, because $\mathbf p(\beta)$ is not linear in $\beta$

## Two things the score equations say

::: {.notes}
Row one needs an intercept, no penalty, a finite solution. Concavity is a claim here; the Hessian is minus a positive-weighted sum of outer products, which is negative semidefinite; uniqueness needs full column rank; existence is the separable case from week 3. Exercise 3 computes the Hessian.
:::

**Row one is the intercept.** $\sum_i (y_i - \hat p_i) = 0$: the fitted probabilities average to the observed proportion of 1s on the training rows.

**The log-likelihood is concave.** Differentiating once more,
$$
\frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial\beta\,\partial\beta^\top} = -\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\, x_i x_i^\top, \qquad w_i = \hat p_i(\beta)\,\big(1 - \hat p_i(\beta)\big) > 0
$$
Each term is minus a positive weight times $x_i x_i^\top$, a matrix that never points uphill in any direction, so the sum curves downward everywhere: the log-likelihood is concave, and any finite solution of the score equations is its global maximum

What concavity does not give: existence. Week 3's separable case is the case with no finite solution

## Newton-Raphson

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide; the exercise now asks for the update, since the Hessian is on the previous slide.
:::

- Find the roots of a function
- Iteratively approximating the function by its tangent
- Root of the tangent line is used as starting point for next approximation
- See the [animation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_method#/media/File:NewtonIteration_Ani.gif) on [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_method)

**Exercise**: using the gradient and the Hessian from the previous slides, derive the Newton-Raphson update for $\beta$ (notebook, exercise 3)

## Logistic regression fitting: multivariate case

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide. Compress if short: each Newton step is a weighted least squares fit; the weights are largest near one half. g is the logit link from week 3.
:::

Newton-IRLS (equivalent) steps, with $g$ the logit link:

$$
\begin{eqnarray}
\hat{\mathbf p}_t & = & g^{-1}(\mathbf X \hat \beta_t)
& \ \text{ update probs.} \\
\mathbf W_t & = & \text{diag}[\hat{\mathbf p}_t (1 - \hat{\mathbf p}_t)]
& \ \text{ update weights} \\
\hat{\mathbf{y}}_t & = & g(\hat{\mathbf p}_t) + \mathbf W_t^{-1}(\mathbf y - \hat{\mathbf p}_t)
& \ \text{ update response}
\end{eqnarray}
$$

and then update parameter estimate (LS sub-problem)
$$\hat{\beta}_{t+1} = \arg \min_{\beta} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_t - \mathbf X \beta)^T \mathbf W_t (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_t - \mathbf X \beta)$$

. . .

**Note**: larger weights on observations with $\hat p$ closer to 1/2, i.e. the most difficult to classify (***look for variations of this theme***) [See Section 4.4.1 of [ESL](https://web.stanford.edu/~hastie/ElemStatLearn/)]{.source}

## GLMs in `R`: what you should know

::: {.notes}
Compress if short: glm fits every family by IRLS (Fisher scoring, which is Newton for these links), in a handful of iterations; a boundary warning means investigate, not necessarily that the MLE does not exist (a finite MLE with a huge slope triggers it too). The reason the rest of the world does not do this is the p by p Hessian: part 2.
:::

**Does `glm` use Newton-Raphson for every family?** Its fitter is IRLS, which is Fisher scoring: Newton with the expected Hessian in place of the actual one. For the default links (`binomial`-logit, `poisson`-log, `gaussian`-identity) the two coincide; for other links it is a close relative. `lm` is the one-step case

**How many iterations?** Usually under ten. `summary()` prints `Number of Fisher Scoring iterations`

**When does it fail?** Mostly when there is no finite MLE, week 3's separable case, with coefficients growing at every iteration. The warning `fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred` is a symptom to investigate, not a diagnosis: a finite MLE with a steep slope triggers it too

**Why does the rest of machine learning not do this?** Each step solves a $p \times p$ system. For $p$ in the millions that is the cost that matters; the next part avoids it

::: {.notes}
Compress: every method so far is a loss, a class, and an algorithm. From here on the algorithm is gradient descent, and usually its stochastic version.
:::

### Part 2: gradient descent

#### ML $\approx$ ERM $+$ SGD

## ML tasks as optimization problems

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide in the course notation. Three choices: loss, class, algorithm.
:::

For a given **loss function** $\ell(y, f(x))$ and **probability model** $(X,Y) \sim P$, we want to find a function $f$ to minimize **risk**:

$$
\underset{f}{\text{minimize }}\ R(f) = \mathbb E_P[\ell(Y, f(X))]
$$

. . .

#### Math model $\leftrightarrow$ Statistical model

Assume an i.i.d. sample from $P$, focus on *empirical risk minimization* (**ERM**)

$$
\underset{f \in \mathcal F}{\text{minimize }}\ \hat R_n(f) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \ell(y_i, f(x_i))
$$

. . .

We also choose a **function class** $\mathcal F$ (or parameter set), i.e. a *class of functions* $f$, determining the *domain of the optimization*

## Examples: linear regression, GLM

::: {.notes}
Legacy slides, one slide. For a GLM the loss is minus one row's log-likelihood, so -l/n is the empirical risk of the log loss.
:::

**Linear regression.** Probability model: errors $\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$. Loss: squared, $\ell(y, f(\mathbf x)) = (y - f(\mathbf x))^2$. Class: $\mathcal F = \{ f_\beta(\mathbf x) = \mathbf x^T \beta : \beta \in \mathbb R^{p+1} \}$. Algorithm: OLS, closed form (memorized yet?)
$$\underset{\beta \in \mathbb R^{p+1}}{\text{minimize }} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \mathbf x_i^T \beta)^2$$

. . .

**GLM.** Probability model: `family = binomial(), poisson(), etc`. Loss: minus one row's log-likelihood, so $\hat R_n(\beta) = -\ell(\beta)/n$. Class: $\{ g^{-1}(\mathbf x^T \beta) : \beta \in \mathbb R^{p+1} \}$, link $g$ fixed. Algorithm: ERM (here also MLE) by Newton-Raphson or gradient descent
$$
\underset{\beta \in \mathbb R^{p+1}}{\text{minimize }} -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \log L(\beta ; y_i | \mathbf x_i)
$$

## Optimization algorithms

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide. Hessian is p by p; gradient is p by 1.
:::

Downside of Newton-Raphson: requires second derivatives, including *inverting the $p \times p$ Hessian matrix* when optimizing over $p > 1$ parameters

If $p$ is large, **second-order** optimization methods like Newton's are very costly

. . .

First order methods only require computing the $p \times 1$ gradient vector

Recall that the gradient is a vector in the *direction of steepest increase* in the parameter space

## Gradient (steepest) descent

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide, with the course symbols: beta_t for the iterates (n is the sample size), gamma the step size.
:::

i.e. skiing as fast as possible. Notation: the objective is the empirical risk $\hat R_n(\beta)$, and $t$ counts steps

1. Start at an initial point $\beta_0$

2. For step $t = 1, \ldots$

    - Compute $\mathbf d_t = \nabla \hat R_n(\beta_{t-1}) \color{#b73779}{\text{ (gradient)}}$

    - Update $\beta_{t} = \beta_{t-1} - \gamma_t \mathbf d_t$

3. Until some **convergence criteria** is satisfied

. . .

Where the **step size** $\gamma_t > 0$ is made small enough to not "overshoot" and increase the loss, i.e. the loss only decreases

## Which step size?

::: {.notes}
One minute, a show of hands per option. Most get 0.05 right (slow) and are surprised that 0.18 converges through the zigzag and 0.21 blows up.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r}
#| label: valley
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| out-width: "100%"
contour_plot(gd_path(c(-4, 1.2), 0.15, 25))
```
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
A valley, $f(\beta) = \tfrac12(\beta_1^2 + 10\beta_2^2)$, ten times steeper across than along. Gradient descent from the orange point with $\gamma = 0.15$

The direction is right locally and wrong globally: a few zigzags across, then a crawl along
:::
:::

::: {.ask}
Same valley, same start, three step sizes: $\gamma = 0.05$, $\gamma = 0.18$, $\gamma = 0.21$. For each, commit: converges, converges slowly, or diverges?
:::

## Three step sizes

::: {.notes}
Third panel shows eight steps; the rest are off the page. Say it: the largest curvature sets the largest safe step, the smallest sets how long it takes.
:::

```{r}
#| label: three-steps
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-width: 12
#| out-width: "100%"
p1 <- contour_plot(gd_path(c(-4, 1.2), 0.05, 25), "0.05: 25 steps, still crawling")
p2 <- contour_plot(gd_path(c(-4, 1.2), 0.18, 25), "0.18: zigzag, converges")
p3 <- contour_plot(gd_path(c(-4, 1.2), 0.21, 8), "0.21: diverges")
p1 + p2 + p3
```

Across the valley the update multiplies $\beta_2$ by $1 - 10\gamma$: $0.5$, $-0.8$, $-1.1$

## The quadratic case, exactly

::: {.notes}
Read the slide. The ratio is the condition number, the word can be said. For gamma between 1/a_1 and 2/a_1 the steep direction can be the slow one (0.18 on the valley: factors 0.8 and 0.82). Least squares: the curvatures are the eigenvalues of 2 X'X / n.
:::

One direction with curvature $a > 0$: $f(\beta) = \tfrac12 a\beta^2$, $\nabla f = a\beta$, so

$$
\beta_{t+1} = \beta_t - \gamma a\beta_t = (1 - \gamma a)\,\beta_t, \qquad \beta_t = (1 - \gamma a)^t \beta_0
$$

Converges iff $|1 - \gamma a| < 1$, i.e. $0 < \gamma < 2/a$. The step $\gamma = 1/a$ lands in one move

. . .

Several directions with curvatures $a_1 \ge \dots \ge a_p > 0$, one step size for all of them: $\gamma < 2/a_1$ to converge, and the slowest direction shrinks like $\max_j |1 - \gamma a_j|^t$, which for $\gamma \le 1/a_1$ is $(1 - \gamma a_p)^t$

::: {.leave}
The largest curvature sets the safe step; the ratio $a_1/a_p$, the shape of the valley, sets the speed (a direction with $a_j = 0$, as in least squares with $p > n$, never moves). For least squares, $\hat R_n(\beta) = \frac1n\|\mathbf y - \mathbf X\beta\|^2$, the $a_j$ are the eigenvalues of $2\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X/n$
:::

## {.inverse .center}

::: {.notes}
Compress: the loop computes one number each step, the gradient; this part is about what that number can and cannot tell you.
:::

### Part 3: what the gradient is telling you

## Reading the gradient

::: {.notes}
The gradient is zero at the minimum, but also at a local minimum, on a plateau (nearly), and at a saddle. Large means steep, and a step may overshoot. The question for the part: when the loss stops falling, which of these are you at?
:::

```{r}
#| label: landscape-1d
#| fig-height: 2.4
#| fig-width: 11
#| out-width: "100%"
# A one-parameter loss with a steep wall, a local minimum, a shallow monotone plateau (slope about -0.01)
# and the global minimum: two Gaussian wells, two exponential walls and a gentle tilt. Its stationary
# points are the two minima and the local maximum between them (checked numerically, 17 October).
f1 <- function(x) 2.5 - 1.0 * exp(-(x + 3.5)^2 / 0.4) - 2.5 * exp(-(x - 2.5)^2 / 0.8) + exp(-2.5 * (x + 5.3)) + exp(2.5 * (x - 4.3)) - 0.01 * x
g1 <- function(x) 1.0 * exp(-(x + 3.5)^2 / 0.4) * (2 * (x + 3.5) / 0.4) + 2.5 * exp(-(x - 2.5)^2 / 0.8) * (2 * (x - 2.5) / 0.8) - 2.5 * exp(-2.5 * (x + 5.3)) + 2.5 * exp(2.5 * (x - 4.3)) - 0.01
x_lmin <- optimize(f1, c(-4.5, -2.5))$minimum; x_gmin <- optimize(f1, c(1.5, 3.5))$minimum
curve1 <- tibble(x = seq(-6, 4.6, length.out = 400)) |> mutate(f = f1(x))
marks <- tibble(x = c(-5.3, x_lmin, -1.0, x_gmin),
                label = c("steep: large gradient", "local minimum: zero", "plateau: nearly zero", "global minimum: zero")) |>
  mutate(f = f1(x), slope = g1(x))
ggplot(curve1, aes(x, f)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, colour = v_blue) +
  geom_segment(data = marks, aes(x = x - 0.5, xend = x + 0.5, y = f - 0.5 * slope, yend = f + 0.5 * slope), colour = m_orange, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = marks, aes(x, f), colour = m_orange, size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = marks, aes(x, f + 0.9, label = label), size = 4.5, colour = v_dark) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-1.5, 7)) + labs(x = expression(beta), y = "loss")
```

Each step computes one thing about where it stands, the gradient $\nabla \hat R_n(\beta_t)$, and its size says little on its own: **zero** at the minimum, but also at a local minimum, and nearly zero on a plateau; **large** means steep, and a step may overshoot

::: {.ask}
Your loss has stopped falling. Which of the four are you at, and how would you tell?
:::

## Landscapes

::: {.notes}
Left: three starts on the same loss, same step size, three places after 60 steps: the local minimum, barely moved on the plateau (it reaches the global minimum after about 500 steps, panel B later), the global minimum. Right: the saddle; a start on the u = 0 line goes to the saddle and stays. Convex losses, least squares and logistic regression, have none of this; most of what comes after week 7 has all of it.
:::

```{r}
#| label: landscapes
#| fig-height: 3.1
#| fig-width: 12
#| out-width: "100%"
gd1 <- function(x0, gamma, steps) { x <- x0; out <- numeric(steps + 1); out[1] <- x
  for (t in 1:steps) { x <- x - gamma * g1(x); out[t + 1] <- x }; tibble(start = as.character(x0), step = 0:steps, x = out, f = f1(out)) }
paths1 <- bind_rows(gd1(-5.3, 0.25, 60), gd1(-1.0, 0.25, 60), gd1(4.2, 0.25, 60))
pa <- ggplot(curve1, aes(x, f)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(data = paths1, aes(x, f, colour = start), size = 1.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = filter(paths1, step == 0), aes(x, f, colour = start), size = 3.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(v_dark, v_teal, m_orange)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-1.5, 7)) + labs(x = expression(beta), y = "loss", title = "three starts, same step size, 60 steps") + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15))
fs <- function(u, v) (u^2 - 1)^2 + v^2
gds <- function(start, gamma, steps) { b <- start; out <- matrix(NA, steps + 1, 2); out[1, ] <- b
  for (t in 1:steps) { b <- b - gamma * c(4 * b[1] * (b[1]^2 - 1), 2 * b[2]); out[t + 1, ] <- b }
  tibble(start = paste(start, collapse = ","), step = 0:steps, u = out[, 1], v = out[, 2]) }
sgrid <- expand_grid(u = seq(-1.8, 1.8, length.out = 121), v = seq(-1.4, 1.4, length.out = 101)) |> mutate(f = fs(u, v))
paths2 <- bind_rows(gds(c(0, 1.2), 0.1, 60), gds(c(0.15, 1.2), 0.1, 60), gds(c(-0.15, 1.2), 0.1, 60))
pb <- ggplot() + geom_contour(data = sgrid, aes(u, v, z = f), breaks = c(0.05, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2.5, 4), colour = "grey70") +
  geom_path(data = paths2, aes(u, v, group = start, colour = start), linewidth = 0.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = paths2, aes(u, v, colour = start), size = 1.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = filter(paths2, step == 0), aes(u, v, colour = start), size = 3.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = 0, shape = 4, size = 5, stroke = 1.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(v_dark, v_teal, m_orange)) + coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "u", y = "v", title = "the saddle at the cross") + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15))
pa + pb + plot_layout(widths = c(1.15, 1))
```

::: {.ask}
Right: $f(u, v) = (u^2-1)^2 + v^2$. Compute the gradient at $(0, 0)$; is it a minimum? The teal path starts at $(0, 1.2)$: where does it end, and why does it never leave?
:::

Where you start decides where you end. Least squares and logistic regression have one valley (convex); most of what comes after week 7 does not

## Too big, too small

::: {.notes}
Left: the penguins with gamma = 12, above 2/L = 8: the loss gets worse and then sits at 0.77, bouncing between two points; flat and not converged (the logistic gradient is bounded, so this is a step-size problem, not an exploding gradient). Right: the landscape's plateau from beta = -1; the gradient is about 0.01, the loss is flat for 400 steps, then drops. Exploding and vanishing gradients are a chain-rule phenomenon, named only.
:::

```{r}
#| label: big-small
#| fig-height: 2.9
#| fig-width: 12
#| out-width: "100%"
pg <- penguins |> filter(species != "Gentoo") |> drop_na(flipper_length_mm) |>
  mutate(chinstrap = as.numeric(species == "Chinstrap"), z = as.numeric(scale(flipper_length_mm)))
Xl <- cbind(1, pg$z); yl <- pg$chinstrap; nl <- nrow(Xl)
L_logit <- max(eigen(t(Xl) %*% Xl / nl)$values) / 4
logloss <- function(b) { z <- Xl %*% b; mean((1 - yl) * z + log1p(exp(-z))) }
run_logit <- function(gamma, steps) { b <- c(0, 0); out <- numeric(steps)
  for (t in 1:steps) { p <- 1 / (1 + exp(-Xl %*% b)); b <- b - gamma * (-t(Xl) %*% (yl - p) / nl); out[t] <- logloss(b) }
  tibble(gamma = paste("step", gamma), step = 1:steps, loss = out) }
big <- bind_rows(run_logit(4, 40), run_logit(12, 40))
pc <- ggplot(big, aes(step, loss, colour = gamma)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(v_blue, m_orange)) +
  labs(x = "step", y = "log loss", colour = NULL, title = "too big: penguins, 2/L = 8") + theme(legend.position = "top", plot.title = element_text(size = 15))
xp <- -1.0; plateau <- numeric(800); for (t in 1:800) { xp <- xp - 0.25 * g1(xp); plateau[t] <- f1(xp) }
pd <- ggplot(tibble(step = 1:800, loss = plateau), aes(step, loss)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, colour = v_blue) +
  labs(x = "step", y = "loss", title = "too small: the plateau, gradient 0.01") + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15))
pc + pd
```

**Too big** a step and the loss rises or bounces: the valley at $\gamma = 0.21$, the penguins at $\gamma = 12$. **Too small** a gradient and nothing moves for hundreds of steps, then everything does

A different mechanism with a similar look, named and not derived: in a deep network the chain rule multiplies derivatives across layers, and the product can be enormous or negligible: **exploding** and **vanishing** gradients

## Has it converged?

::: {.notes}
Simulated, first 200 steps only: A is the quadratic valley, converged; B is the landscape from beta = -1, on the plateau; C is the valley with the geometric step schedule 0.3 (0.6)^t, whose steps sum to a finite distance, so it stopped short. Take answers before the reveal.
:::

```{r}
#| label: converged-data
#| include: false
qa <- gd_path(c(-4, 1.2), 0.15, 800) |> mutate(loss = fq(b1, b2) + 0.3)
lb <- plateau
bc <- c(-4, 1.2); lc <- numeric(800); for (t in 1:800) { bc <- bc - 0.3 * 0.6^t * c(1, 10) * bc; lc[t] <- fq(bc[1], bc[2]) + 0.3 }
conv <- bind_rows(tibble(panel = "A", step = 1:800, loss = qa$loss[-1]),
                  tibble(panel = "B", step = 1:800, loss = lb),
                  tibble(panel = "C", step = 1:800, loss = lc))
# The 200-step view keeps each panel's full vertical range, so that B's plateau looks flat rather than zoomed in.
conv_plot <- function(d) ggplot(d, aes(step, loss)) + geom_blank(data = mutate(conv, step = 1)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, colour = v_blue) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 200, linetype = "dotted") + facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_y") + labs(x = "step", y = "training loss")
```

```{r}
#| label: converged-200
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| fig-width: 12
#| out-width: "100%"
conv_plot(filter(conv, step <= 200))
```

Simulated: three runs of gradient descent, 200 steps each, and all three losses are flat. One has converged to its minimum; one is on a plateau; one has a step size that shrank to nothing on the way

::: {.ask}
Which is which? What would you check, and what would you do next?
:::

## Has it converged? The next 600 steps

::: {.notes}
The reveal. A was converged; B drops after about 450 steps; C never moves again. A flat loss was consistent with all three. Two different jobs: the gradient norm and restarts diagnose the optimization; held-out data (next week) decide when to stop for prediction, which is a different question.
:::

```{r}
#| label: converged-800
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| fig-width: 12
#| out-width: "100%"
conv_plot(conv)
```

A converged (the valley). B was on the plateau and drops at step `r min(which(lb < 2))`. C stopped short: its steps $0.3 \cdot 0.6^t$ sum to a finite distance

At step 200 the three were indistinguishable, and no theorem below would have told them apart. In practice, two different jobs: the **gradient norm**, restarts from elsewhere and running longer diagnose the optimization; **held-out data** decide when to stop for prediction, which is next week's question

## Curvature

::: {.notes}
The ingredient the lemma needs. We know the quadratic case exactly; a general f is quadratic to second order, so a step has a first-order term we like and a second-order term we do not control.
:::

::: {.recall}
Taylor, to second order: for a smooth $f$ and a small move $\delta$, $f(x + \delta) \approx f(x) + \nabla f(x)^\top\delta + \tfrac12\,\delta^\top \nabla^2 f(x)\,\delta$.
:::

What decides whether a step helps is how fast the gradient changes along it. Take the step $\delta = -\gamma\nabla f(x)$ and write $g = \nabla f(x)$:
$$
f(x - \gamma g) \approx f(x) \;\underbrace{-\; \gamma\,\|g\|^2}_{\text{always down}} \;\underbrace{+\; \tfrac12\gamma^2\, g^\top \nabla^2 f(x)\, g}_{\text{the curvature pushes back}}
$$

In the quadratic case the curvature was a fixed number $a$. On the landscapes above it changes from place to place: $+2$ at the bottom of a valley, $-4$ at the saddle, about $0$ on the plateau

## Curvature at most $L$

::: {.notes}
If curvature is at most L everywhere, the push-back is bounded and the quadratic rule survives. "Curvature at most L" without a Hessian: the gradient changes at rate at most L. Least squares: L = 2 lambda_max(X'X)/n. The saddle example has no global L: its curvature 12u^2 - 4 is unbounded.
:::

If the curvature in every direction is at most $L$ in size, the push-back is at most $\tfrac12 L\gamma^2\|g\|^2$, and then
$$
f(x - \gamma g) \lesssim f(x) - \gamma\big(1 - \tfrac12 L\gamma\big)\|g\|^2
$$
The bracket is positive for $\gamma < 2/L$ and the bound is best at $\gamma = 1/L$: the quadratic case's rule, in general

. . .

To make it a theorem, say "curvature at most $L$" about the gradient, with no second derivative:

**Assumption.** $\nabla f$ is **$L$-Lipschitz** for some $L > 0$: $\|\nabla f(x) - \nabla f(y)\| \le L\,\|x - y\|$ for all $x, y$

A quadratic with curvatures $a_j$ has $L = \max_j |a_j|$, the valley's $a_1$; least squares, $L = 2\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)/n$; the saddle example has no single $L$ (curvature $12u^2 - 4$ in $u$)

## Descent lemma

::: {.notes}
The one positive result, and what it does and does not say. It needs no convexity; it says each step helps, by an amount proportional to the squared gradient; it does not say where you end up, and a small gradient means slow progress, not arrival.
:::

::: {.leave}
**Descent lemma.** If $\nabla f$ is $L$-Lipschitz, then for every $x$
$$
f\!\left(x - \tfrac1L\nabla f(x)\right) \le f(x) - \frac{\|\nabla f(x)\|^2}{2L}
$$
Every step of size $1/L$ decreases $f$ by at least the squared gradient over $2L$ (strictly, unless $\nabla f(x) = 0$).
:::

The one guarantee, and its price. It says: no convexity needed; each step helps, more where the gradient is large. It does not say the steps converge (on $f(x) = -x$ they walk off forever); if they do, the limit is a stationary point, any of the landscape's. A small gradient is not arrival: the next step gains little, which is the plateau

Proof: integrate the gradient along the step, and let the Lipschitz bound do what the curvature bound did

## Descent lemma, proof (1 of 2)

::: {.notes}
(a) We have f(y) - f(x); we want the gradient in it: integrate the gradient along the segment from x to y.
(b) We want the first-order term on its own: add and subtract the gradient at x.
(c) The leftover is where the assumption goes: Cauchy-Schwarz, then Lipschitz; x_t - x has length t times the step.
:::

Write $v = y - x$ for the step, so that $y = x - \gamma\nabla f(x)$ means $v = -\gamma\nabla f(x)$, and $x_t = x + tv$ for the point a fraction $t$ of the way along it, so that $\|x_t - x\| = t\|v\|$

$$
\begin{alignedat}{2}
f(y) - f(x) &= \int_0^1 \nabla f(x_t)^\top v\, dt
&\quad& \class{fragment}{\color{gray}\small\text{(a) along the step}} \\
&\class{fragment}{{}= \nabla f(x)^\top v + \int_0^1 \big[\nabla f(x_t) - \nabla f(x)\big]^\top v\, dt}
&& \class{fragment}{\color{gray}\small\text{(b) add and subtract}} \\
&\class{fragment}{{}\le \nabla f(x)^\top v + \int_0^1 \|\nabla f(x_t) - \nabla f(x)\|\,\|v\|\, dt}
&& \class{fragment}{\color{gray}\small\text{(c) Cauchy-Schwarz}} \\
&\class{fragment}{{}\le \nabla f(x)^\top v + \int_0^1 L\,t\,\|v\|^2\, dt}
&& \class{fragment}{\color{gray}\small\text{(d) Lipschitz}}
\end{alignedat}
$$

## Descent lemma, proof (2 of 2)

::: {.notes}
(e) Integrate t. (f) Put the step in: v is minus gamma times the gradient. Then read off the sign.
:::

$$
\begin{alignedat}{2}
f(y) - f(x) &\le \nabla f(x)^\top v + \int_0^1 L\,t\,\|v\|^2\, dt
&\quad& \\
&\class{fragment}{{}= \nabla f(x)^\top v + \tfrac{L}{2}\|v\|^2}
&& \class{fragment}{\color{gray}\small\text{(e) } \textstyle\int_0^1 t\, dt = \tfrac12} \\
&\class{fragment}{{}= -\gamma\|\nabla f(x)\|^2 + \tfrac{L}{2}\gamma^2\|\nabla f(x)\|^2}
&& \class{fragment}{\color{gray}\small\text{(f) } v = -\gamma\nabla f(x)} \\
&\class{fragment}{{}= -\gamma\big(1 - \tfrac12 L\gamma\big)\|\nabla f(x)\|^2}
&& \class{fragment}{\color{gray}\small\text{(g) collect}}
\end{alignedat}
$$

. . .

At $\gamma = 1/L$ the right-hand side is $-\|\nabla f(x)\|^2/2L$, which is the lemma. $\blacksquare$

For any $0 < \gamma < 2/L$ the right-hand side is $\le 0$, and $< 0$ unless $\nabla f(x) = 0$: every such step decreases $f$ until the gradient vanishes, and the heuristic's bound was right

## Logistic regression by descent

::: {.notes}
Same loop, only the gradient function changed. The Hessian from part 1 is at most X'X/4n, so L is an eighth of least squares' 2 lambda_max/n; here 2/L is 8, which is why 12 bounced. Convex, so this is the benign case: one valley, and the lemma's step lands in it.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
#| label: logistic-descent
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| out-width: "100%"
b <- c(0, 0); Tn <- 25; path <- matrix(NA, Tn, 2)
for (t in 1:Tn) { p <- 1 / (1 + exp(-Xl %*% b)); b <- b - 4 * (-t(Xl) %*% (yl - p) / nl); path[t, ] <- b }
glm_coef <- coef(glm(chinstrap ~ z, family = binomial, data = pg))
tibble(step = 1:Tn, intercept = path[, 1], slope = path[, 2]) |>
  pivot_longer(-step, names_to = "coefficient") |>
  ggplot(aes(step, value, colour = coefficient)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = glm_coef, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "step", y = "coefficient", colour = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "top")
```
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
Chinstrap against Adelie from flipper length (standardized), penguins data, from $\beta_0 = (0, 0)$, step $\gamma = 4$

Objective: $\hat R_n(\beta) = -\ell(\beta)/n$. Gradient, from part 1: $-\mathbf X^\top(\mathbf y - \mathbf p(\beta))/n$

Same loop as least squares; only the gradient changed. Dotted: `glm`'s answer

Curvature: $w_i \le \tfrac14$ in part 1's Hessian, so $L = `r round(L_logit, 2)`$ here and $2/L = `r round(2 / L_logit, 1)`$. One valley: the benign case
:::
:::

## {.inverse .center}

::: {.notes}
Compress: one exact gradient per step is too expensive at scale; a random row's gradient is cheap and, on average, right.
:::

### Part 4: stochastic gradient descent

## What a step costs

::: {.notes}
With the linear cost model: full gradient at the 2012 scale about 7e13 operations, a batch of 128 about 8e9, ten thousand times cheaper. For a network the per-image cost is not p, but the ratio n/b is what matters. The formula's p-cubed is not a computation anyone has done.
:::

Second-order methods invert the $p \times p$ Hessian; first-order methods compute the $p \times 1$ gradient. For a linear model or a GLM, where one row's gradient costs about $p$ operations:

| | Operations | Once or per step? |
|---|---|---|
| Least-squares formula $(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y$ | about $np^2 + p^3$ | once |
| One gradient-descent step | about $np$ | per step |
| One step on a random batch of $b$ rows | about $bp$ | per step |

::: {.ask}
$n = 1{,}200{,}000$ images, $p = 60{,}000{,}000$ parameters. If one image's gradient cost about $p$ operations, roughly how many is one full gradient? And one step on a batch of 128?
:::

## Stochastic/random descent

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide; the derivation is on the next slide, over the random index with the data fixed. Ask first, then reveal.
:::

- Instead of computing the gradient of the loss function on the entire dataset, compute it on a random sample

::: {.ask}
Pick one row $I$ uniformly at random from $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ and use its gradient $\nabla\ell_I(\beta)$ in place of the average over all $n$ rows. Commit: is it biased for the full gradient $\nabla\hat R_n(\beta)$, yes or no?
:::

## The stochastic gradient is unbiased

::: {.notes}
Derived in one line. Only the index is random; the data and beta are fixed, so nothing about where the data came from is used. Without replacement the variance is smaller by the finite-population factor; week 2's seminar met that factor.
:::

With the data and $\beta$ held fixed, only $I$ is random, and by linearity of $\nabla$, $\mathbb E$ and $\sum$,
$$
\mathbb E_I\big[\nabla\ell_I(\beta)\big] = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac1n\,\nabla\ell_i(\beta) = \nabla\hat R_n(\beta)
$$

Unbiased, whatever the data are. A batch of $b$ rows drawn independently with replacement averages $b$ such gradients: still unbiased, with variance $\sigma^2(\beta)/b$, where $\sigma^2(\beta)$ is the spread of the single-row gradients

Compute update using one randomly sampled observation, or a randomly sampled subset ("mini-batch SGD")

## The two paths

::: {.notes}
Simulated least squares. An epoch is one pass through the rows, 200 single-row steps, so the orange path is three epochs. Blue is exact and expensive; orange is cheap and noisy, and with a shrinking step the noise ball shrinks. Do not say "SGD is better": say what each costs and what each buys. Cut 2 if short.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| label: two-paths
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-width: 6
#| out-width: "100%"
set.seed(9)
ns <- 200; x1 <- rnorm(ns); x2 <- 0.6 * x1 + 0.8 * rnorm(ns); Xs <- cbind(x1, x2); ys <- Xs %*% c(2, -1) + rnorm(ns)
ols <- solve(t(Xs) %*% Xs, t(Xs) %*% ys)
Ls <- 2 * max(eigen(t(Xs) %*% Xs / ns)$values)
bg <- c(-2, 2); gdp <- matrix(NA, 31, 2); gdp[1, ] <- bg
for (t in 1:30) { bg <- bg - (1 / Ls) * (-2 / ns * t(Xs) %*% (ys - Xs %*% bg)); gdp[t + 1, ] <- bg }
bs <- c(-2, 2); sgp <- matrix(NA, 601, 2); sgp[1, ] <- bs
for (t in 1:600) { i <- sample(ns, 1); bs <- bs - (0.05 / (1 + t / 100)) * (-2 * Xs[i, ] * (ys[i] - sum(Xs[i, ] * bs))); sgp[t + 1, ] <- bs }
pgrid <- expand_grid(b1 = seq(-2.5, 3.5, length.out = 101), b2 = seq(-2.5, 2.5, length.out = 101)) |>
  mutate(f = map2_dbl(b1, b2, ~ mean((ys - Xs %*% c(.x, .y))^2)))
ggplot() +
  geom_contour(data = pgrid, aes(b1, b2, z = f), breaks = min(pgrid$f) + c(0.05, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16), colour = "grey75") +
  geom_path(data = as_tibble(sgp, .name_repair = ~ c("b1", "b2")), aes(b1, b2), colour = m_orange, alpha = 0.8, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_path(data = as_tibble(gdp, .name_repair = ~ c("b1", "b2")), aes(b1, b2), colour = v_blue, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(data = as_tibble(gdp, .name_repair = ~ c("b1", "b2")), aes(b1, b2), colour = v_blue, size = 1.8) +
  annotate("point", x = ols[1], y = ols[2], shape = 4, size = 5, stroke = 1.5) +
  coord_equal() + labs(x = expression(beta[1]), y = expression(beta[2]))
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
Simulated least squares, $n = 200$, two inputs

**Blue:** 30 full gradient steps, $6{,}000$ row-gradients. **Orange:** 600 single-row steps, $600$ row-gradients, step $0.05/(1 + t/100)$

The noisy path reaches the neighborhood of the answer ($\times$) for a tenth of the work, and never sits still. With noise the step shrinks, $\gamma_t \to 0$, but not so fast that it stops short (panel C): Robbins and Monro, 1951
:::
:::

Compress: the algorithm is done; what is left over, and where does it come from?

### Part 5: what the fitting leaves over

## Early stopping

::: {.notes}
Legacy slide. Optimization time is a knob like k or the polynomial degree.
:::

#### Optimization time = complexity

- For many optimization algorithms the fitted model becomes more complex the longer the optimization algorithm runs

. . .

  - e.g. the more steps of (stochastic) gradient descent used in combination with a flexible function class

  - e.g. the more steps of forward stepwise (adding more predictor variables)

. . .

**Idea**: control model complexity by stopping the algorithm before convergence

This is [early stopping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_stopping) -- we'll come back to it later

## Stopping early

::: {.notes}
Simulation; the picture the week points at. The algorithm does what it was asked, minimize the training error, and the training error is the wrong thing to minimize all the way. Next week: by how much it lies. Lambda: week 7.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| label: early-stopping
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| out-width: "100%"
set.seed(12)
ne <- 80; pe <- 60
Xe <- matrix(rnorm(ne * pe), ne, pe); be <- rnorm(pe, sd = 0.5); ye <- Xe %*% be + rnorm(ne, sd = 3)
Xh <- matrix(rnorm(2000 * pe), 2000, pe); yh <- Xh %*% be + rnorm(2000, sd = 3)
Le <- 2 * max(eigen(t(Xe) %*% Xe / ne)$values)
bb <- rep(0, pe); es <- vector("list", 300)
for (t in 1:300) {
  bb <- bb - (0.5 / Le) * (-2 / ne * t(Xe) %*% (ye - Xe %*% bb))
  es[[t]] <- tibble(step = t, training = mean((ye - Xe %*% bb)^2), `held-out` = mean((yh - Xh %*% bb)^2))
}
es <- bind_rows(es)
best_step <- es$step[which.min(es$`held-out`)]
es |> pivot_longer(-step, names_to = "error") |>
  ggplot(aes(step, value, colour = error)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(m_orange, v_blue)) + scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "gradient-descent step (log scale, from step 1)", y = "mean squared error", colour = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "top")
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
Simulated: least squares from $\beta_0 = \mathbf 0$, $n = 80$, $p = 60$, noise sd 3, step $1/2L$; held-out error on 2,000 new rows from the same model

Training error falls at every step. The held-out error falls, turns at step `r best_step`, and ends far above its minimum

The number of steps is a tuning parameter, like $k$ or $d$. Week 7 writes the penalty down, $\hat R_n(\beta) + \lambda\|\beta\|^2$, with $\lambda$ as the knob
:::
:::

## Where the error comes from, this time

::: {.notes}
Stated; the two-line proof (add and subtract R(f_F); each bracket is nonnegative by the definitions of f_F and f*) is exercise 2, which also shows that for squared loss the approximation term is E[(f_F - f*)^2] by the optimal model theorem. Three functions: the best of all, the best in the class, what the algorithm returns. The class is chosen before the data; so is the approximation error. Next week starts here.
:::

Three functions. $f^\star = \arg\min_f R(f)$: the best of all (squared loss: week 2's conditional mean). $f_{\mathcal F} = \arg\min_{f \in \mathcal F} R(f)$: the best in the class, fixed once $\mathcal F$ is. $\hat f = \arg\min_{f \in \mathcal F} \hat R_n(f)$: what the data give, random

**Bias--variance decomposition, ERM form.** Both terms are $\ge 0$:
$$
R(\hat f) - R(f^\star) = \underbrace{\big[R(\hat f) - R(f_{\mathcal F})\big]}_{\text{estimation}} + \underbrace{\big[R(f_{\mathcal F}) - R(f^\star)\big]}_{\text{approximation}}
$$

::: {.leave}
Proof: exercise 2, two lines. The class was chosen before the data, and so was the approximation error; the estimation error is the sample's (and can hold bias as well as variance). The same trade-off as week 1's, for any method that minimizes over a class. Next week starts here
:::

## No free lunch

::: {.notes}
Stated (Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, Theorem 5.1, in expectation form); the finite-domain proof is exercise 4. Intuition to say: the sample says nothing about labels at points it has not seen; on a large domain those labels can be set against the method. Comes back in weeks 9 and 11.
:::

**No free lunch (stated).** No method has lower error than every other on every distribution. Binary classification, 0--1 loss: for any learning method and any training size $n$, on a domain with at least $2n$ points there is a distribution for which a perfect predictor exists and the method's expected error (over training samples) is at least $1/4$

What it says: choosing a method is an *assumption* about the world; the ERM form shows where one such assumption enters, the class $\mathcal F$ chosen before the data. What it does not say: that methods are equally good on the problems we meet, or that an assumption is a flaw

::: {.ask}
In the week 1 seminar a line and $k$ nearest neighbors often scored within a standard error of each other on gapminder. A fact about the methods, or about the data?
:::
